# Behaviour question sheet — `james-habits-app`

**3 decisions · 8 reviews.** Generated by `node kit.js sheet james-habits-app --rev james-habits-app@e75de89`, over the app at `james-habits-app@e75de89`. Do not hand-edit — re-run it.

## What this is

Kit read this app's `docs/DESIGN.md` and its backend test names and built one list of
behaviours from both. Everything it read out of the **code** is marked unreviewed until a
human rules on it, because an inference that quietly becomes a specification is the failure
this whole thing exists to prevent.

The two sections below are not the same job and should not take the same effort:

- **Decisions** — Kit can prove both answers change something: either nothing documented
  displays this surface, or two behaviours contradict each other about one value. Each one
  carries the evidence, the options, my recommendation, and the strongest case against it.
- **Reviews** — the code asserts this, a documented screen needs it, and it looks right.
  One line each. If one is wrong, it becomes a decision.

## Brief for the assistant (paste this too)

> You are helping the product owner **pressure-test** these decisions, not make them. For each:
> argue the case *against* the recommendation as strongly as you can; say which option you would
> pick and why in one sentence; and name anything the evidence does not settle. Do not invent a
> third option unless the two on offer genuinely miss the point — and if you do, say which

## Decisions — 3

### D1. The two sides only contradict each other on paper — the route is caller-supplied DEFAULTING to 30, which satisfies both. The real collision underneath is the NAME: DESIGN.md documents ?days=30, the route binds ?historyDays. Which one is the contract the frontend gets built against?

**Why this is a decision:** two behaviours state different values for `region:CompletionGrid.days`.
Both sides were read out of a document rather than out of code, so this is the spec
disagreeing with itself, not the code drifting from it. Kit detects the collision; what it
means is the question above.

| behaviour | says `region:CompletionGrid.days` is | source |
|---|---|---|
| `BEH-WINDOW-MVP` The history window is 30 days | `30` | `docs/DESIGN.md#mvp-5` |
| `BEH-WINDOW-API` The history window is whatever the caller asks for | `caller-supplied` | `docs/DESIGN.md#architecture-api` |

**Also on the table here** — these are part of this question, which is why they are not
in the review list below:

- `BEH-HISTORY-3` The history window parameter is named historyDays, not days — the query parameter is `historyDays`, and `?days=` is silently ignored (`backend/Balenthiran.Habits.WebApi/Routes/HabitRoutes.cs:68`)

**Options**

- **Rename the code to days** — HabitRoutes.cs:68 binds `int days = 30` and HabitApiTests.cs:182 follows. A frontend written from DESIGN.md then works. It is a breaking query-parameter change to a route, and the generated API client needs regenerating.
- **Rename the design to historyDays** — DESIGN.md:83 becomes ?historyDays=30. No code moves, no client regenerates, nothing can break. The document a human and an assistant read to build the screen gets the uglier of the two names.

**I'd pick: Rename the code to days.** This is the cheapest it will ever be: the history screen is habits#13, unbuilt, so there is no consumer to break today and exactly one after it lands. And your own frontend-first rule points this way — the parameter is named by what the screen asks for, not by a handler's local variable. The response body already returns a `days` array, so ?days=7 returning seven days reads as one idea rather than two.

**The strongest case against that:** Nothing is actually broken right now: the default is 30 either way, so the only caller that gets hurt is one written from the doc that also passes the parameter, and none exists. Editing one line of prose is a strictly smaller change than editing a route, a test and a regenerated client, and it carries no chance of breaking a deploy. `historyDays` is also the more explicit name at the call site — `?days` sitting next to a `days` array in the response can read as though it filters that field rather than sizing it. And 'rename it now while it is free' is the argument that gets made immediately before the first consumer appears.

**Your answer** — becomes: the two `provides` lines on `BEH-WINDOW-MVP` and `BEH-WINDOW-API` reconciled — corrected, merged into one statement, or one of them removed, whichever your answer implies.

### D2. Should the Manage screen gain a view of archived habits, or should the includeArchived flag go?

**`BEH-ARCHIVE-2` — Archived habits can be asked for explicitly**

**Why this is a decision:** you said the API layer is inferred from what the UI needs to
display. This surface exists in the code and **no documented screen displays it**, so either
the design is missing a screen or the surface should go. Those are opposite edits.

**Evidence** — read out of `backend/Balenthiran.Habits.Tests/HabitServiceTests.cs:GetAll_excludes_archived_unless_asked`:

- GET /api/habits takes a flag that includes archived habits

**Options**

- **Add the view** — DESIGN.md MVP 4 gains an archived view. The flag earns a documented reason to exist and the frontend gets something to build. More surface on an app whose screens are not built yet.
- **Delete the flag** — GetAll stops taking it and one backend test goes with it. Archived habits stay retrievable by id (BEH-ARCHIVE-1), so nothing is lost — but un-archiving through the UI becomes a new decision if you ever want it.

**I'd pick: Add the view.** Archiving is already a one-way door in the UI: DELETE archives rather than deletes, so a habit archived by mistake is reachable from no documented screen. The flag is not spare surface — it is the missing half of a capability MVP 4 already promises.

**The strongest case against that:** MVP 4 promises archiving, not un-archiving, and none of the three screens exists yet — this adds scope to an app whose Today screen is not built. Deleting the flag costs one test, and the day you want the view you write it then against a design that states it. Keeping unused surface because it might be needed is exactly how an API grows features nobody asked for.

**Your answer** — becomes: `serves BEH-…` added to `BEH-ARCHIVE-2` (with the screen written into `DESIGN.md`), or `BEH-ARCHIVE-2` deleted along with the surface it describes.

> 

### D3. Nothing documented displays an error. Should DESIGN.md gain an error state the frontend renders these into, or should the machine-readable code go and a status code be the whole contract?

**`BEH-ERROR-1` — An unknown habit is a 404 carrying a machine-readable error code**

**Why this is a decision:** you said the API layer is inferred from what the UI needs to
display. This surface exists in the code and **no documented screen displays it**, so either
the design is missing a screen or the surface should go. Those are opposite edits.

**Evidence** — read out of `backend/Balenthiran.Habits.Tests/ProblemDetailsResponseTests.cs:Not_found_returns_a_problem_details_body_with_error_code`:

- GET, PUT, DELETE and history for an unknown habit id all return 404
- the body is ProblemDetails and carries an error code
- an unexpected exception is a 500 that exposes nothing

**Options**

- **Document the error state** — DESIGN.md gains a row saying what each screen shows when a habit 404s and when the API 500s. The error code earns a purpose — the frontend maps code to copy. Costs a design edit now, and commits three screens that do not exist yet to per-code messages.
- **Drop the code, keep the status** — ProblemDetails stays, the bespoke code goes, and one backend test simplifies. The frontend shows one generic failure. You lose the ability to tell 'this habit was archived' apart from 'that id was never real' without adding the code back later.

**I'd pick: Document the error state.** A 404 here is not an exotic path — it is a direct consequence of A5. DELETE archives rather than deletes, so any list the client is holding can name an id the backend now refuses. Undocumented means the frontend author invents the behaviour at the keyboard, which is the thing this corpus exists to stop.

**The strongest case against that:** A6 says single user, and a single user on a single device reaches that stale-id race close to never — so the case above is largely hypothetical, and it is being used to add scope to an app whose Today screen is not built. There is also a cheaper middle this question does not offer: document ONE generic error state, leave the code in the payload unconsumed, and decide per-code copy on the day a second code actually distinguishes something. Picking the full version now spends design effort on branches that may never be rendered.

**Your answer** — becomes: `serves BEH-…` added to `BEH-ERROR-1` (with the screen written into `DESIGN.md`), or `BEH-ERROR-1` deleted along with the surface it describes.

## What Kit is NOT asking you here

Worth stating, because a sheet that omits its own scope reads as complete:

- **The behaviours this app has documented but not built.** Kit refuses to generate a test for a
  screen that does not exist and names the missing noun instead. That list is a build backlog,
  not a question — it goes to zero on its own as the frontend lands.
- **Anything read out of a document you wrote.** A defined behaviour is not up for adjudication
  here; you already ruled on it by writing it down. It only reappears if it collides with
  another defined behaviour — which is exactly what D1 is.
